title: The AI-DRM protocol to enhance the lifetime of wireless sensor network
author: Anand, V

steps.title: Design sensor node schematic
steps.instruction: Create the sensor‑node schematic in Fritzing using a Node MCU (ESP32) powered by a battery; include TX, RX and GPIO pins and colour‑code connections for easy breadboard layout.

steps.title: Assemble sensor node hardware
steps.instruction: Place the components from the schematic on a breadboard (or miniaturise on a PCB) according to the colour‑coded pins, connect the battery, and verify all connections.

steps.title: Design sink node schematic
steps.instruction: Create the sink‑node schematic in Fritzing (unlimited power supply) with the same ESP32 module, TX/RX pins and a Secure Digital (SD) card interface for data logging.

steps.title: Assemble sink node hardware
steps.instruction: Build the sink node on a breadboard or PCB following the schematic, connect it to a stable power source, and attach the SD‑card module.

steps.title: Program nodes with Arduino IDE
steps.instruction: Open the Arduino IDE, select the COM3 port, upload firmware that reads RSSI values from the ESP32 radio and writes the readings to the SD card on the sink node.

steps.title: Measure RSSI versus distance
steps.instruction: Place the sensor node and sink node at a chosen distance d (starting with no obstacles) and record the RSSI value; repeat for increasing distances up to 300 m and optionally with obstacles, logging each measurement on the SD card.

steps.title: Prepare MATLAB simulation parameters
steps.instruction: In MATLAB, set the AI‑DRM simulation parameters as follows: 110 sensor nodes, packet size 1024 bits, simulation area 100 × 100 m², communication range 30 m, sink coordinators 50 and 120, traffic pattern CBR, and run for 2000 rounds.

steps.title: Execute Dynamic Radio Power Consumption Algorithm
steps.instruction: For each transmission event, apply Algorithm 1:

substeps.instruction: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance d between the transmitting sensor and its neighbour.
2. If d ≤ Max_Tx_Range, compute PTX using the Free‑Space Path model.
3. If PTX ≤ Max_PTX and PTX ≥ Min_PTX, accept PTX as the transmission power; otherwise, declare the destination out of range.
• idle_energy = IdlePower × IdleTime; add to total
• sensing_energy = SensingPower × SensingTime; add to total
• PTX_energy = PTX_power × PTX_time; add to total
• PRX_energy = PTX_power × PRX_time; add to total
• WSN_total_energy_consumption = Σ total_energy_consumption[i] for all nodes i
• Multiply by rerouting factor 1.2 and overhead factor 0.5 as needed:
6. End the algorithm for the current round.

steps.title: Collect and analyse simulation results
steps.instruction: After completing 2000 rounds, extract from MATLAB the number of alive nodes, cluster‑head (CH) formations, residual energy percentages, throughput and packet‑drop ratios; compare these metrics with the ARORA and EACHS‑B2SPNN protocols as shown in the article figures.

description: WSNs can be used for important tracking and monitoring tasks, such as border, sea, and forest monitoring. Because WSNs are deployed in areas that are inaccessible to humans and their sensors run on batteries, their lifespan presents significant research challenges. Therefore, recharging and replacement of the battery are not possible. This WSN requires a protocol that can efficiently use the energy of all sensor nodes without wasting it because the nodes are deployed at random. In the current WSN scenario, all the sensor nodes consume identical amounts of energy without concentrating on the distance from the next node or the packet size. In this work, two sensor nodes are created using microcontrollers and other hardware to collect real-time data for the prediction of transmission power, and the prediction technique is applied while simulating the WSN. The RSSI values are measured while moving both nodes at different distances via the Arduino IDE’s COM3 port. The mobile sensor nodes are shown in Fig. 1 below, and the sink node is shown in Fig. 2. When the distance between nodes increases, the signal strength (RSSI) decreases. In the proposed protocol, the collection of real-time RSSI data plays a major role in the prediction and simulation of the WSN to increase its lifetime.Fig. 1Mobile sensor node.Fig 1Fig. 2Sink node.Fig 2 Customised Prototype: The prototype for the sink node and sensor node, shown in Fig. 1, Fig. 2, is a customised prototype designed using the Fritzing non-profit organisation application (Fig. 3, Fig. 4) and developed in the laboratory to meet the research objectives. These prototypes make a major contribution to fetching real-time datasets and tuning sensor nodes to consume only the required energy for transmission, based on the data size and distance.The sensor node prototype is powered by a battery and can operate over different distances ‘d’.
